# Coder task 011 — fix the 009 C2 destination-eviction path (it hangs the board)

**Opened 2026-09-24.** Thinker → coder. Do not edit this file; write everything in `REPORT.md`.
Starting point: **`739bd2a`** on branch `sbc-sampling` (009 C2 as committed). All prior work is committed.

> ⚠️ **Nothing in section 4 is proven.** Section 3 is board evidence and is solid. Section 4 is an RTL
> review: six suspected defects, each with a stated confidence. Exactly one (F1) is provable by reading
> a single line; the rest are arguments, not measurements. **Treat them as leads to verify, not as a
> defect list to apply blind.** If a gate shows a lead is wrong, that is a finding — report it and stop.

---

## 1. Why this task exists, in one paragraph

Task 010 ran a board bisection and found that the **009 C2 build (`739bd2a`) hangs the FPGA** on
`520.omnetpp_r` with migration ON: **0 completions in 4 runs** under `policy=plru`, and 3 of 4 under
`random`. A wedge is a hard freeze — zero bytes on the serial line, no kernel output, board unusable
until reprogrammed. The 008 C2 build (`e41f780c67ff` = commit **`201ebae`**, proven from archived git blob hashes —
010 §8.4) runs **the same workload, the same policy, the same protocol, to completion**. The 009 Verilator gate was green, so the
sim does not catch this. This task finds and fixes the cause.

## 3. The evidence (task 010, board, 64 KB single-core, `520.omnetpp_r --sim-time-limit=0.002s`)

### 3.1 The split is by RTL, not by policy

| build | commit | policy | pass | wedge |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| #3 `e41f780c67ff` | **`201ebae`** (008 C2) | random | 2 | 0 |
| **#3 `e41f780c67ff`** | **`201ebae`** (008 C2) | **plru** | **1** | **0** |
| #5 ≡ #6 ≡ #7 `ced7fdc79ee7…` | **`739bd2a`** (009 C2) | random | 3 | 1 |
| #5 ≡ #6 ≡ #7 `ced7fdc79ee7…` | **`739bd2a`** (009 C2) | **plru** | **0** | **4** |

#5, #6 and #7 are **one bitstream** — byte-identical configuration data, only the embedded build
timestamp differs (010 §2). So the 4 PLRU wedges and the 1 random wedge are all the same bits.

The #3 PLRU run is the control: `ITER_RC=0`, `ITER_SECS=1029`, 17 heartbeats, none missed, in the exact
configuration that fails 4/4 on `739bd2a` — first and only workload run of a fresh boot, `parked=0
migrations=0` verified before arming, read-back `migrate : ON` / `policy : plru`.

### 3.2 The mechanism split, measured in the same 0.7 s window

At `HB t=0s`, both builds had done comparable SBC work — #3: 7,767 migrations / 548,806 accesses;
#7: 7,211 / 570,845 — but:

| `0x498` / `0x4A0` / `0x4A8` at `t=0s` | #3 (008-c2) | #7 (009-c2) |
|---|---:|---:|
| what the registers mean in that build | destination **aborts** | destination **W evictions** |
| value | **0 / 0 / 0** | **2,938 total** |
| result of the run | **completed** | **wedged** |

Over #3's whole run those registers reached 21,814 — so 008-c2 *met* a dirty or client-held destination
way 21,814 times and **declined every one**. It never probed a destination way and never Released one.
009-c2 evicts them. **The build that never executes the new path completes; the build that runs it
2,938 times in 0.7 s wedges.**

### 3.3 Sanity of the measurement

All five identities exact on the control run: `accessA` = the four outcomes; `dataMiss + upgradeMiss =
memReads + memAcqPerm`; `secondSearch = secondaryHit + secondaryMiss`; `L2_Cycles ÷ 50e6` = the
heartbeat clock; and **K3** (`attempted − migrations = dstAbortDirty + Held + Both`) = 21,814 = 21,814.
K3 fails by design on 009, so its holding proves from the counters alone that the control ran on 008-c2
RTL — no hash argument needed.

### 3.4 Why the wedges arrive late in a run, not at once

The destination read raises `preferInvalid`, so W is evicted **only when row D has no invalid way**.
Destination sets fill gradually, which is why wedges land after thousands of migrations (7,211 and
11,411 in the two captured cases) rather than immediately.

## 4. The six suspected defects

Each row: the RTL, what is wrong, confidence, the proposed fix. **Verify before you apply.**

### 4.0 What tasks 008 and 009 already recorded, and why it matters here

Read before the leads — three entries in the existing record carry most of the weight.

**(a) The invariant 009 broke is written down in the RTL, next to the code that avoided it.**
`MSHR.scala:512-516`, at `io.status.bits.migPending`:

> *"Deliberately NOT folded into `dstValid` — no destination is reserved yet, and fencing the
> destination set before the probe completes would add a hold-and-wait edge (**"migration holds set d
> while waiting on the L1"**) that the baseline does not have."*

009 C2 does **exactly that**: it raises `dstValid` and then waits on the L1 for W's ProbeAck. 009's own
TASK §4.4 admits it ("the hold-and-wait edge the design has avoided until now") and offers `nestD` as
the mitigation. **So the only question is whether `nestD` is wide enough — which is lead F2.**

**(b) `bug-fix-log.md` P1 was closed by REMOVAL, and only for the partner set.**

> *"closed in 003 Stage 2c (`ac7253d`) — **by removal, not by patch**: the way-lock protects the parked
> way, so the **partner-set** term left `dstSetConflict` and a `Release` can no longer stall the C head."*

The **`dstSet`** term never left — `Scheduler.scala:277` still carries it, and its comment says so:
*"The dstSet terms STAY … Victim protection is now the way-lock's; occupancy is still this."* A client
`Release` to row D can therefore still stall the head of the C channel, which is why the C-head
watchdog (`Scheduler.scala:448-450`, *"C-channel head held by the destination/partner fence (bug P1)"*)
was **kept**. That watchdog is sim-only. **P1 is not closed for the destination set; it was only made
unreachable, by never waiting on the L1 while the destination fence is up. 009 removed that property.**

This also raises F3: P1's closure argument rests on *"the way-lock protects the parked way."* The
destination way W **gets no way-lock** (F3), so it has neither the old fence protection nor the new one.

**(c) 008 F7 is the frequency multiplier — the probe path is common, not rare.**
008 REPORT F6/F7 measured what D's least-recent line actually is: in the C2 stress test, **43,972
destination aborts against 20 migrations**, and the reasons were **clean-but-client-held 40,369
(91.8%)**, dirty+held 3,219 (7.3%), dirty-only 384 (0.9%). Its unchecked guess: *"most client bits on
D's least-recent line are stale (Rocket's L1 drops clean lines without a Release — CLAUDE.md G5; the
source-side probe found them stale 99.99% of the time, `cbb3837`)."*

So under 009 the common case is **probe a client that does not actually hold W**. The L1 answers
`NtoN`, which is legal — but the *round trip* is what matters, because the fence is up for all of it.
On the board this is not a corner: at the wedge, **2,938 of 7,211 migrations (40.7%)** had taken a
dirty or client-held W. Over a full ~4.5 M-migration run that is **~1.8 M exposures** to the
hold-and-wait window. It has to coincide with one L1 write-back to row D **once**.

**(d) A second, independent open bug is live on this path.** 008 F5 = **B8-1** (tracker M19): teardown
races a deferred migration's stale partner claim. Pre-existing in `744fabb`, proven by repro on a
flag-off build, **never fixed**, and 009's TASK §0 told the coder not to fix it. It is a **sim assert,
silent on the FPGA**, live in *both* policies and traffic-dependent. #3 passes, so B8-1 alone is not
the hang — but do not mistake it for one of the leads below if it fires.

### F1 — random mode runs the new code (contradicts 009's own U2) · **confidence: certain**

`MSHR.scala:308`
```scala
val evictW = params.micro.plruReplacement && params.micro.enableSetBalancing
```
A **Scala compile-time** value. The runtime `usePlru` (`L2_Replacement`, `0x490`) is wired to the
Directory (`Directory.scala:195, :211`) and the Scheduler (`Scheduler.scala:211`) but **never reaches
the MSHR at all** — the MSHR has no such input. So `takeW = evictW.B && !dstFree` (`MSHR.scala:1647`)
fires in random mode too, and the abort branch it replaced is dead in this build whatever is written to
`0x490`.

009 decision **U2**: *"Do not change random mode in any way (U2) — including its silent overwrite of a
clean destination way."* It is changed. This is also the cleanest explanation of the single random-mode
wedge: the Directory's clean-way tier still hands random a clean, client-free W, so random gets the
**Release** half of the new path but rarely the **probe** half — matching `dstAbort*` = 0 in random
against 2,938 in PLRU, and 1/4 against 4/4.

**Fix:** add a `usePlru` input to the MSHR and make it a runtime decision —
`val takeW = io.usePlru.getOrElse(false.B) && !dstFree` — with the abort branch restored for random
mode. Keep the "PLRU never aborts" assert, gated on `usePlru`. Zero hardware when
`plruReplacement = false`.

### F2 — the C-channel escape hatch closes too early · **confidence: high**

`MSHR.scala:501`
```scala
io.status.bits.nestD := dstEvict && !w_dprobeackfirst && !dstMeta.displaced
```
`nestD` is what lets an L1 `Release` addressed to row D reach the C MSHR instead of jamming the head of
the inner C channel. It is true **only while W's probe is unanswered**, and drops on the *first*
ProbeAck beat.

The fence on D (`dstValid`) stays up far longer: W's Release, the outer `ReleaseAck`, the copy,
dir-write #1, the `Acquire`, the `Grant`, the `GrantAck`. Through all of that a `Release` to row D
cannot be consumed — `allocReady` is fenced, no MSHR matches set D, so `nestC` is false and
`request.ready` is false (`Scheduler.scala:277, 290, 314-317, 433`) — and it stops **all** inner C
traffic behind it. SinkC gates a voluntary Release on `io.req.ready` but a ProbeAck only on the
BankedStore queue (`SinkC.scala:144`), which is bug P1's exact shape.

009 TASK **I3** argues no cycle forms because *"the migrant needs nothing from the L1 C channel to
retire."* That holds for one transaction in isolation. 009 stretched the window by a memory round trip,
and Rocket arbitrates its probe unit and its writeback unit onto that single C channel.

**See §4.0(a) and (b):** this is the one edge the pre-009 design deliberately never had, P1 is still
open for the destination set, and §4.0(c) makes the exposure ~1.8 M events per run rather than rare.
**This is the primary suspect.**

**Fix:** widen the window to the whole eviction —
`dstEvict && !(w_dprobeacklast && w_dreleaseack)`, or simply `dstEvict`. N5 (`Scheduler.scala:121-128`)
already stalls the migrant while the C MSHR is in row D, so the H2/H7 ordering argument still holds.

### F3 — the destination way W is never way-locked · **confidence: high**

`MSHR.scala:549-554`
```scala
val lockBorrowed = !s_sinval || inPlace
io.status.bits.lockValid := lockBorrowed || (meta_valid && !meta.hit && meta.state =/= INVALID)
io.status.bits.lockSet   := Mux(lockBorrowed, pairSetReg, physSet)
io.status.bits.lockWay   := Mux(lockBorrowed, secWay,     meta.way)
```
Each MSHR locks exactly **one** way: its borrowed way in the partner set, or its own victim in its own
row. `(migDstSet, migDstWay)` is neither. So while the migrant is probing and Releasing W — now a long,
protocol-visible operation — nothing tells the Directory that way is occupied
(`Scheduler.scala:496-500` builds `busyWays` from those fields). Tolerable before 009, when W was
overwritten in a couple of cycles.

**Fix:** a second lock slot covering `(migDstSet, migDstWay)` while `dstEvict`. Update the reasoning
behind `Directory.scala`'s `assert(freeWays.orR)` and the "at most two ways in a row are locked"
comment, which this changes.

**Why this is more than tidiness (§4.0(b)):** P1 was closed on the argument that *the way-lock*
protects a way somebody is inside. W is the one way that is being operated on for hundreds of cycles
and is **not** covered by it.

### F4 — `allowDisplacedVictim` is a no-op · **confidence: medium (latent trap, not the hang)**

`Directory.scala:200` is its only use, inside `evictableOH` → tier 1. Tier 1 is
`evictTier = preferEvictable && !usePlru` (`:211`), and `preferEvictable` is raised **only** for the
migration destination probe (`Scheduler.scala:490`) — where `allowDisplacedVictim` is always true. So
the flag is true wherever it is reachable and ignored everywhere else.

The Scheduler comment claiming *"only the migration destination probe may take a parked way as its
victim — a source read must never pick a guest, because the AT records one hop only"* therefore
describes a rule **nothing enforces**. It happens to hold for a different reason (a guest picked on a
demand miss is Released, not migrated), but it sits directly against the standing hard rule never to
weaken a `displaced` test.

**Fix:** either apply the mask to the policy and free-way tiers as well, or delete the flag and correct
the comment. **Do not leave it as is.** Say in the REPORT which you chose and why.

### F5 — 009's N2 was downgraded from a fix to an assert · **confidence: medium**

009 TASK **N2** required adding `|| (dstEvict && !w_dprobeackfirst)` to the MSHR's `nestC`, so that a
`Release` of a **guest** W (whose address maps to S, the migrant's own set) nests rather than queuing.
The implementation skipped it and substituted, `MSHR.scala:1374`:
```scala
assert (!probingW || io.status.bits.nestC, "009: nestC is false while W's probe is open (Q2)")
```
The reasoning — that `nestC`'s `!w_grantfirst` term (`MSHR.scala:511`) is incidentally true all through
a migration, because the demand `Acquire` is gated on `w_dread && w_copy` (`:621`) — does hold today. It
is a coincidence between two unrelated pieces of logic, and the only thing guarding it is an assert
that is **not in the bitstream**.

**Fix:** implement N2 as 009 specified. Keep the assert as a check, not as the mechanism.

### F6 — the `ReleaseAck` split is by order, not identity · **confidence: medium-low**

`MSHR.scala:1436`
```scala
.elsewhen (io.sinkd.bits.opcode === ReleaseAck) {
  when (!w_dreleaseack) { w_dreleaseack := true.B } .otherwise { w_releaseack := true.B }
}
```
Both Releases use `source = 0`, so they are told apart purely by which wait-flag is still low — and
`w_dreleaseack` goes low at the **directory result**, before the Release is sent. Correct only while the
T6 assert holds, and T6 is not synthesized. If it is ever wrong the MSHR retires with W's Release
unacknowledged, drops the fence, and the next `Acquire` for W's address goes out: a **T5 violation** on
the outer link.

**Fix:** distinguish them by something real — a distinct source id, or a bit set when the message is
actually accepted by SourceC rather than when the wait is armed.

### F7 — one data-corruption path to rule out in sim · **confidence: unproven, needs a run**

A freeze with no serial output fits corrupted kernel memory as well as a protocol deadlock.
`SourceC.scala:89`
```scala
io.bs_adr.valid := (beat.orR || io.evict_safe) && want_data
```
checks `evict_safe` **only on beat 0**; after that it reads the row unguarded. That is stock behaviour,
but 009 adds new writers to `(D, W)` during exactly that read, and the H3 interlock
(`Scheduler.scala:651-653`) covers only the copy — not SinkC and not SourceD. No reachable interleaving
was constructed during review (our probe of W completes before our Release starts, so the client can no
longer be releasing W). **This is what the shadow checkers exist to catch — settle it with V2, not with
an argument.**

## 5. Decisions the thinker must make before the coder starts

**These are open. Do not assume an answer.**

| # | Question | Options |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | **Fix or revert?** | (a) fix `739bd2a` in place; (b) revert 009 C2 to **`201ebae`** and re-land it later behind the fixes. (b) is now stronger than when this task was drafted: `201ebae` is the commit the passing bitstream was built from (proven, 010 §8.4), so it is a **board-verified** fallback, not just an older one. It costs the 009 feature |
| D2 | **Scope.** Is F1 alone enough for the first commit? | F1 is one line and provable. It restores random mode to 007-C2 behaviour and would show, in one board pair, whether the remaining fault is confined to the probe/Release path |
| D3 | **F4** — mask the other tiers, or delete the flag and fix the comment? | Changing the mask alters victim selection in both policies and is a performance change, not just a safety one |
| D4 | **Is the "at most one way locked per MSHR" invariant negotiable?** F3 needs a second slot | `Directory.scala`'s `freeWays.orR` assert rests on it. With ways = 16 there is ample room; the *proof* is what changes |

## 8. Board run — the only check that matters

The sim gate was green for 009 C2 and the board still hung. **A green V0–V6 does not close this task.**

- Image: 64 KB single-core PLRU, built from the final commit. Archive under task + commit,
  `cmp`-verified, and **record the sha256 in the REPORT, not the filename** (010 §9.1: three archived
  files there turned out to be one bitstream).
- Protocol, per 010: fresh boot, verify `migrations=0 parked=0` **by read-back** before arming, then
  `--reset-all --migrate=on`, confirm read-back on **lines 2–3** of `sbc_read` (`head -1` cannot show
  `migrate`), `--zero` on the run, and watch with the manual heartbeat loop.
- **Target: 4 consecutive PLRU ON completions.** 009 wedges 4/4, so 4 passes is the smallest sample
  that inverts the result. Runs are ~17 min each and several fit in one boot; the boot is the expensive
  part (~45 min).
- Also run 4 in `random`, because F1 means random's behaviour changes too.
- Report `memReads` and `memWrites` **separately**, plus `SBC_DstDirty/Held/Both`, `attempted`,
  `migrations`, `parked`, and whether **K3** holds (it must not, in PLRU, if the eviction path is live).

⚠️ **If it wedges, capture 010 TASK §6 before reprogramming.** Reprogramming destroys the only view
into the failure.

---

## 9. Do not

- Do not treat section 4 as proven. A failing lead is a **finding to report**, not a thing to work around.
- Do not fix a failing gate by tweaking the test.
- Do not remove or weaken the destination fence, the migration token, `s_wsafe`, or any `w.displaced` test.
- Do not reorder BankedStore priorities.
- Do not reuse the stock probe/release registers, `probes_done`/`probes_toN` or `meta` for W (009 §4.3).
- Do not repoint `status.way` / `status.physSet` (009 N7).
- Do not add a new MMIO register or counter without asking (009 U6 still stands).
- Do not fix B8-1, M17 or M18 here. Do not tune thresholds.
- Do not `git checkout` whole files — uncommitted configs live in this tree.

## 10. Open, carried from 010

1. **008-c2 is a strong suspect's alibi, not a proven one.** #3 has **one** PLRU pass. `739bd2a` passed
   3 of its first 4 random runs before wedging. Three more PLRU runs on #3 would turn 1/1 into a rate.
   Until then, "009 broke it" is supported but thin.
2. **The random wedge rate is bounded, not measured** — 1 in 4.
3. Candidates #1, #2 and #4 from 010 were never run.
